newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Kohl arrives for tropical Australian break.
newsitem.headline: Kohl arrives for tropical Australian break.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl arrived in Australia's tropical north on Friday, kicking off a five-day official visit with a weekend of rest and recreation on the Great Barrier Reef.
Kohl, the West's longest-serving leader, flew to the city of Cairns on a German air force Airbus from Brunei accompanied by about 50 business people.

He was greeted by federal tourism minister John Moore -- Australia hopes Kohl's weekend in Queensland will attract more wealthy German tourists -- before heading north for the palm-lined resort of Port Douglas.

"Germany is one of our fastest-growing European tourist markets, with more than 125,000 German people choosing Australia as the place to holiday in 1996," Moore said in a statement before Kohl's arrival.
"The visit by Chancellor Kohl to important tourist destinations will also increase international awareness of Australia's great attributes," Moore added.
Kohl, 67, is following in the footsteps of U.S. President Bill Clinton, who visited Cairns and Port Douglas last November soon after his re-election.
His activities this weekend will largely mirror those of Clinton -- visiting the Great Barrier Reef and the rain forest of far north Queensland.

On Sunday evening Kohl and his business delegation will fly south to the Australian capital Canberra for a day of talks on Monday with political leaders including Prime Minister John Howard, who received Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week.
The talks are expected to focus on strengthening trade ties.
Germany is Australia's ninth-largest trading partner with the trade balance going in favour of the European economic powerhouse.

Australian exports to Germany, mostly primary products such as wool and iron ore, totalled A$1.2 billion in the 1995/96 financial year but imports left a A$3.7 billion trade gap, according to official figures.
One international issue likely to be on the agenda -- as it was with both Clinton and Hashimoto -- will be the need for binding international controls on greenhouse gas emissions.

Howard's conservative coalition, elected 13 months ago, has shifted from the policy of the previous Labor administration on the need for compulsory targets to cut emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, arguing that such targets would damage Australian industry.

But Germany is at the forefront of a European plan to toughen the scheme at the third international Climate Change conference in Kyoto, Japan, in December and the United States has also put pressure on Canberra to fall into line on the issue with its Western allies.
Kohl's visit to Australia is his second since he became Chancellor in 1982 but his first since German reunification.
Kohl will round off his visit on Tuesday with a day in Sydney when he is expected to take a trip around the city's harbour before flying to New Zealand early on Wednesday.
